intro/hello: Welcome to neural networks. In this chapter, we finally build one.
intro/recap: Remember the linear classifier from Chapter 4: one matrix multiply, W times x.
intro/walls: Its boundaries are straight walls, and on these three classes, wound into a spiral, straight walls get only about half the points right.
intro/horse: Images hit the same limit. One template per class cannot say: a horse facing left, or a horse facing right.
intro/fix: The fix is the neural network, built from pieces you already have: matrix multiplies, a simple bend between them, and backprop to train it all.
intro/bent: Same spiral, small network. The walls bend to follow the arms.
intro/plan: First the plain math, then the brain analogy behind the name, then the design choices: which activation, how many layers, and how wide.
two-layer/formula: A two layer neural network does two multiplies instead of one, with a very simple function in between.
two-layer/x: Flatten an image into a vector of three thousand and seventy two numbers.
two-layer/w1: The first matrix, W one, has a hundred rows, each a template, as in a linear classifier. Out come a hundred numbers.
two-layer/max: Now the bend: the max of zero and each number. Negatives become zero, positives pass straight through.
two-layer/hidden: What survives is the hidden layer, h: a hundred features the network computes for itself.
two-layer/w2: A second matrix, W two, combines them into ten class scores.
two-layer/or: Now the network can say or: this is a horse if template seventeen fires, or if template forty two fires.
two-layer/learned: Both matrices are learned by gradient descent and backprop. The hundred is our choice: a hyperparameter.
two-layer/bias: Real layers also add a bias vector, left out here to keep the picture clean.
collapse/why: Why bother with the max? What if we leave it out?
collapse/assoc: Then it computes W two times W one times x, and we can move the brackets.
collapse/one: W two times W one is just another matrix, ten by three thousand and seventy two. Call it W.
collapse/disguise: So the network collapses into one linear classifier in disguise. NumPy agrees: the answers match exactly.
collapse/with: Put the max back, and they no longer match.
collapse/toy: To see what the max buys, shrink it down: one input, three hidden units, one output.
collapse/lines: Each hidden unit computes a straight line of x. The max folds it at zero into a hinge: flat on one side, sloped on the other.
collapse/sum: Add the hinges with the output weights, and the result bends wherever a hinge does.
collapse/straight: Without the max, a sum of lines is just a line, with no bend. More hidden units, more bends: that is how a network curves its boundaries.
collapse/three: A three layer network repeats the pattern: multiply, bend, multiply, bend, multiply.
neuron/name: The field began by modeling the brain, and the vocabulary stuck.
neuron/cell: The basic computing cell of the nervous system is the neuron. A human brain has about eighty six billion of them.
neuron/syn: They are wired together by a hundred trillion to a quadrillion connections, called synapses.
neuron/parts: A neuron gathers signals through branching dendrites, and sends its own down one long axon, which branches to other neurons.
neuron/model: The classic model turns this into arithmetic.
neuron/mul: A signal x crossing a synapse is multiplied by its strength, a weight w: positive to excite, negative to inhibit. Learning adjusts these weights.
neuron/sum: The cell body adds up the weighted inputs, plus a bias: a dot product.
neuron/fire: If the total is high enough, the neuron fires. The model keeps only the firing rate, computed by an activation function, f.
neuron/sig: Historically, that was the sigmoid, squashing any total into a rate between zero and one.
neuron/coarse: But this model is very coarse. Real neurons come in many types, dendrites compute on their own, and spike timing matters.
neuron/math: So treat the brain as loose inspiration. A neural network is a mathematical function.
one-neuron/known: With the right loss attached, one neuron is already a classifier you know.
one-neuron/score: Its weighted sum, w dot x plus b, is a linear score. Here, w is an arrow, and the score grows in the direction it points.
one-neuron/sig: The sigmoid squashes the score into the probability of class one: orange where the neuron is sure, blue where it is sure of class zero.
one-neuron/train: Train it with the cross entropy loss, minus the log probability of the right class, and the arrow swings around to fit.
one-neuron/logreg: This is logistic regression, the two class softmax classifier from Chapter 4. With a hinge loss instead, it is a binary support vector machine.
one-neuron/pred: Either way, it predicts class one exactly when the score is positive. The boundary is the straight line where the score is zero.
one-neuron/reg: One more look, at regularization. The L two penalty adds lambda times w to each weight's gradient.
one-neuron/regroup: Regroup the update: each step first multiplies every weight by a number just below one, then applies what the data asks for.
one-neuron/forget: Here, that number is zero point nine nine five. Switch off the data, and the arrow shrinks, the boundary blurs: the neuron slowly forgets.
one-neuron/keep: Weights the data keeps reinforcing survive, the rest decay: regularization is gradual forgetting.
squash/why: Every neuron applies a fixed nonlinearity, and the choice matters: in backprop, the gradient through a neuron is multiplied by its local slope.
squash/sig: First, the sigmoid, the classic choice. It squashes any input into zero to one, like a firing rate.
squash/tails: Push z out to five, and the curve is nearly flat. Its slope is zero point zero zero seven, so the gradient from above is cut to under one percent.
squash/peak: Even at its steepest, in the middle, the slope is only a quarter.
squash/sat: A saturated neuron passes almost no gradient back, so learning stalls. And weights that start too large saturate most neurons at once.
squash/center: Second, sigmoid outputs are always positive, so the next layer only ever sees positive inputs.
squash/same: Each weight's gradient is its input times one shared number. With all positive inputs, every weight gradient has the same sign.
squash/zig: So the weights all rise together, or all fall. A mixed target takes a zig zag.
squash/tanh: Tan h fixes that. It squashes into minus one to one, centered on zero: a stretched, shifted sigmoid.
squash/still: But it still has flat tails, so it still saturates. Even so, always prefer tan h over the sigmoid.
relu/relu: Now the modern default: the rectified linear unit, ReLU. Zero for negative inputs, the input itself for positive ones.
relu/rect: Rectified is an electronics word: a rectifier lets current through one way only. ray-loo passes positive inputs and blocks negative ones.
relu/fast: It makes gradient descent converge much faster: about six times, in Krizhevsky's twenty twelve network.
relu/why: Its right half never saturates, and it is cheap: a comparison, not an exponential.
relu/die: The catch: ReLU units can die. Each dot is this unit's input on one example. Dots right of zero pass gradient back. Dots left pass nothing.
relu/shove: Now one large update shoves the weights, so the input is negative for every example.
relu/dead: From then on it outputs zero and passes zero gradient, for every example, forever. With too high a learning rate, up to forty percent of a network can die.
relu/leaky: Leaky ReLU gives the negative side a small slope, like zero point zero one, so a unit is never fully off. Results are mixed.
relu/maxout: Maxout goes further: each neuron computes two linear functions, and outputs the larger.
relu/special: ReLU is the special case with one piece fixed at zero. So maxout keeps the good parts and never dies, at twice the parameters.
relu/advice: The advice: use ReLU, mind the learning rate, and watch for dead units.
relu/else: If units die, try leaky ReLU or maxout. Tan h is worth a try, but expect worse. And never use the sigmoid in hidden layers.
layers/org: Networks are organized into layers, each feeding the next, with no cycles.
layers/fc: The common kind is fully connected: each neuron connects to every neuron in the layer before.
layers/count: A naming trap: an N layer network does not count the input. With a hidden layer and an output layer, this one is a two layer network.
layers/single: A single layer network maps inputs straight to outputs, like logistic regression or the SVM.
layers/out: And the output layer usually has no activation: its scores can be any real numbers.
layers/params: Now count what it learns. Each line is a weight: three times four, plus four times two, is twenty. Plus six biases, one per neuron: twenty six parameters.
layers/deeper: Add a second hidden layer of four, and one output. Twelve plus sixteen plus four is thirty two weights, plus nine biases: forty one.
layers/scale: For scale, the convolutional networks later in the course have about a hundred million parameters, across ten to twenty layers.
forward/payoff: Layers pay off in practice: a whole layer is one matrix multiply.
forward/rows: Stack layer one's neuron weights as the rows of a matrix, W one, and their biases in a vector, b one.
forward/line: Then one line, f of W one times x, plus b one, computes every neuron's sum at once, and applies the activation to each entry.
forward/input: Here is a three layer network with real weights: blue wires positive, red negative, thicker for larger. The input is three numbers.
forward/l1: Layer one: each hidden neuron sums its weighted inputs, adds its bias, and applies the sigmoid. One dot product does all four.
forward/l2: Layer two does the same, reading the outputs of layer one.
forward/l3: The output layer is a weighted sum plus a bias, with no activation. That number is the score.
forward/batch: That is the whole forward pass. If x holds a batch of examples as columns, the same lines handle them all at once.
forward/learn: What makes it useful is the right weights and biases. Learning them is the rest of the course.
power/family: A network of fixed shape is a whole family of functions, one per setting of its weights. How rich is that family?
power/rich: Remarkably rich. One hidden layer with enough neurons can approximate any continuous function as closely as you like. That is the universal approximation theorem.
power/target: Let us build one by hand. Here is a wiggly target.
power/step: A steep sigmoid is a step: it jumps from zero to one at a point, a.
power/bump: Subtract a second step at b, and you get a bump: one between a and b, zero elsewhere.
power/stack: Chop the range into six pieces, give each bump the target's height there, and add them up: a network with twelve hidden sigmoids.
power/more: More bumps, and the staircase hugs the target ever closer. The error goes as low as you like.
power/weak: But can represent is a weak promise. It says nothing about how many units you need, or whether gradient descent finds them.
power/deep: In practice, depth helps: deeper networks fit real data compactly and train well. Still, fully connected networks rarely gain beyond three layers.
power/hier: Convolutional networks are the exception: depth is crucial there, perhaps because images are hierarchical. Faces are made of eyes and noses, which are made of edges and blobs.
capacity/q: So how big should a network be?
capacity/cap: More neurons means more capacity. Here is a two layer network on the spiral, with one hidden neuron.
capacity/one: One or two neurons can only crease the plane a couple of times, and accuracy stalls well short of a hundred percent.
capacity/four: With four, the boundary starts winding along the arms. With eight, it gets nearly every point right.
capacity/crease: The boundary is made of straight pieces, creased where hidden units switch on or off. That is ReLU at work.
capacity/cuts: But capacity cuts both ways. Here is a disc of one class inside another, with twelve percent of the labels flipped.
capacity/islands: A big network, fifty neurons with almost no regularization, carves little islands around the mislabeled points.
capacity/overfit: That is overfitting: nearly perfect on training data, worse on anything new.
capacity/small: A small network paints in broad strokes and ignores the odd point. So should we play it safe, with small networks?
big-nets/wrong: No. That conclusion is wrong, for two reasons.
big-nets/tools: First, there are better tools against overfitting than shrinking: L two regularization, dropout, and input noise.
big-nets/same: Same fifty neuron network, same start, with lambda raised to zero point zero one. The islands melt, and the boundary settles toward the true circle.
big-nets/acc: Training accuracy falls, since it stops memorizing noise, but held out accuracy rises. Push lambda much higher, and it underfits.
big-nets/second: Second, and subtler: small networks are harder to train with gradient descent.
big-nets/lottery: Train ten networks of each size from ten random starts, and plot each final loss.
big-nets/spread: With three hidden neurons, the results scatter: some starts do well, others get stuck. With thirty, all ten land at the same low loss.
big-nets/minima: Small networks have fewer local minima, but many are bad. Big ones have more, nearly all equally good, so they do not depend on luck.
big-nets/rule: So the rule: use as big a network as your budget allows, and control overfitting with regularization, tuned on validation data.
outro/stack: To recap: a neural network is layers of multiply, bias and nonlinearity. Without the nonlinearity, it collapses to a linear classifier.
outro/neuron: The brain lent us the name, but the model is a cartoon, and one neuron is a linear classifier.
outro/relu: ReLU is the default activation. Sigmoids saturate, and are not centered on zero.
outro/count: We never count the input layer, the output layer has no activation, and parameters are weights plus biases.
outro/power: One hidden layer can approximate anything, but depth helps. And prefer big networks, kept honest by regularization.
outro/next: Next, how to make these networks train well: how to prepare the data, where to start the weights, and how to keep a big one honest.
